# Non-Response, Attrition and Missing Data {#sec-nonresponse-attrition}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Learning objectives"}
- Distinguish complete observations from recruitment targets.
- Understand why recruitment inflation does not repair bias.
:::

## The idea

If $n_{complete}$ analysable records are required and the anticipated fraction without complete usable data is $L$, a planning approximation is $n_{recruit}=n_{complete}/(1-L)$, followed by appropriate upward rounding. The distinction between an expected loss of observations, failure to enrol and non-adherence matters. Inflation addresses anticipated quantity of usable data; it does not fix systematic differences between participants with and without outcomes.

## When and how to apply it

Different software implementations may inflate an unrounded analytical requirement before applying the ceiling or may first round up the complete requirement. These conventions can differ by one or more recruits. The reporting paragraph should identify the adopted convention, especially when explaining a software-generated answer.

## Formula at a glance

$$
n_{recruit}=\left\lceil\frac{n_{complete}}{1-L}\right\rceil
$$


## Teaching case 1 — baseline draft

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Clinical scenario / initial worked example"}
For 385 **already rounded** complete observations and 10% anticipated unusable records, $\lceil385/0.90\rceil=428$. The calculator currently uses a different preserved convention for some legacy methods: it inflates the unrounded base (384.16), producing 427 in this example.
:::

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Common error"}
Never describe extra recruitment as correction for selection or attrition bias.
:::

## Hands-on exercise

Compare 5%, 10% and 20% expected loss under the same rounding convention and write the adjusted target clearly.

Recruitment inflation protects expected usable counts, but does not remove bias.
